blocks.raw:
<Callout>

Sun shading devices reduce solar heat gain by 40–70% without sacrificing daylighting; they are essential tropical architecture elements. The **brise-soleil** (sun breaker) and related devices—horizontal louvers, vertical fins, egg-crate screens, light shelves, and overhangs—must be designed for Philippine latitude (5°N–20°N) where solar altitude angles are high even in winter. Le Corbusier's Chandigarh Capitol Complex demonstrates brise-soleil geometry creating dynamic facade patterns while controlling solar penetration; this approach integrates climate responsiveness with architectural expression—a model for contemporary Philippine tropical design.
</Callout>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Testable hierarchy for Philippine shading priority: (1) West facade is worst (600–800 W/m², afternoon peak when outside temperature is highest), (2) East facade is second-worst (600–800 W/m², early morning but duration is shorter), (3) South facade is least critical (300–450 W/m², high sun angle reduces penetration depth). Shading design should allocate deepest overhangs to west, adequate-but-less-deep to east, minimal-adequate to south. This priority order is frequently tested.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>The 3,600W calculation (10 m² east window, 600 W/m² incident, 60% transmission) assumes clear-sky conditions. During monsoon (Type I habagat, May–Oct), cloud cover reduces direct radiation 20–40%, making shading less critical. This variation is rarely highlighted but affects BERDE energy modeling—Type III areas with pronounced dry season benefit from seasonal adjustable shading; Type II/IV with perpetual cloud require less aggressive shading to maintain daylighting.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Do not directly apply Chandigarh-derived brise-soleil dimensions to Philippine buildings. The 23° latitude difference means Philippine solar altitudes are much steeper year-round. A shading device designed for 31°N will be grossly oversized at 14.6°N. Always recalculate overhang depth using local solar altitude angles—the LEA tests whether you can distinguish climate-specific design from universal application.</Warn>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Blocking Stack Effect Exhaust. Placing horizontal louvers across roof-level exhaust vents or clerestories, impeding buoyancy-driven ventilation. Natural ventilation effectiveness drops by 40–50%. Always ensure louvers don't block vertical airflow paths.", "Over-Reliance on Motorized Systems. Installing expensive motorized louvers without fixing fundamental design flaws (oversized windows, poor orientation). The building still overheats during electrical failures or sensor malfunctions.", "Inadequate Winter Daylighting. Designing overhangs that block winter diffuse light, forcing daytime electric lighting. Type II/IV climates (perpetual cloud cover) suffer more; Type I (dry season) benefits from deeper shading year-round.", "Misaligned Brise-Soleil Geometry. Copying Chandigarh egg-crate spacing (0.5–0.7 m cells, appropriate for 31°N) in Manila (14.6°N). Result: Oversized cells; insufficient shading for high-altitude tropical sun; poor aesthetic integration."]} />
